explanation: Edison Studios made a short Frankenstein in 1910, 21 years before Boris Karloff's famous monster. Nosferatu, an unlicensed take on Dracula, followed in 1922.

claims.text: Edison Studios released a short film of Frankenstein in 1910.
F. W. Murnau's Nosferatu was released in 1922.
Boris Karloff played the creature in Universal's Frankenstein (1931).
Nosferatu was an unauthorized adaptation of Bram Stoker's Dracula.

writerNotes: Players who picture Boris Karloff's 1931 film reach for Nosferatu, which is the trap. Twelve years apart. Self-check 9.3. Lint: clean. Claims: every claim listed, risk at or above the C26 floor; the schema's riskReason list has no only or counterintuitive, so such claims carry the nearest listed reason. Datasets: no pinned dataset covers film or TV facts, so every high-risk claim here needs checker evidence from the web. Rival test: Arguing for Nosferatu: it is the famous early horror film, but the Edison short is twelve years older. Volatility: evergreen; no time words; nothing depends on events after mid-2026. Regional: the work is known worldwide and the options need no single country's local knowledge. Style: Oxford spelling, straight single quotes, plain hyphens, explanation of 24 words. Myths: claims screened against myths.json, no match. Mystery and encore: not applicable to a practice item. Doubts: the explanation's 21 years is 1931 minus 1910, arithmetic on c1 and c3.

evidence.restatement: Edison's studio released a short Frankenstein in 1910.
